Gastrointestinal Disorders

Nausea and Vomiting

Nausea and vomiting are symptoms, not a diagnosis. The ED job is to stabilize first, then sort benign gastroenteritis from obstruction, CNS disease, pregnancy, metabolic derangement, drug/toxin effect, ACS, and dangerous abdominal disease.

Board trap: Do not let a patient leave just because the nausea improved; antiemetic response does not rule out obstruction, MI, raised ICP, pregnancy complication, DKA, or sepsis.

NAUSEA AND VOMITING

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Most cases are gastrointestinal, but high-yield ED misses come from outside the gut: pregnancy, intracranial lesions or infection, myocardial infarction, diabetic ketoacidosis, adrenal disease, hypercalcemia, thyroid disease, drug toxicity, and cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome. The first branch is stability and red flags, not which antiemetic to order.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Vomiting reflects coordinated activation of the vomiting center through vagal afferents, the chemoreceptor trigger zone, vestibular pathways, cortical input, and visceral pain/inflammation. The receptor pattern explains why no one medication works for every case: serotonin antagonists, dopamine antagonists, antihistamines, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, and prokinetics each fit different pathways.

Pattern matters: acute vomiting suggests infection, obstruction, toxin, pregnancy, CNS, or metabolic disease; chronic vomiting pushes motility, cancer therapy, neurologic, psychiatric, or medication causes; recurrent stereotyped episodes raise cyclic vomiting syndrome or cannabinoid hyperemesis.

CLINICAL FEATURES

HISTORY

Ask onset, timing, frequency, bilious/feculent/bloody content, relation to meals, abdominal pain, headache, neurologic symptoms, vertigo, chest pain, dyspnea, diarrhea, obstipation, fever, travel, food exposure, pregnancy possibility, diabetes, renal disease, prior surgery, malignancy, immunosuppression, alcohol, cannabis, and medication or toxin exposure. Vomiting of food eaten more than 12 hours earlier is a gastric outlet obstruction clue.

Red flags include severe abdominal pain, peritonitis, altered mental status, headache with neurologic findings, chest pain or dyspnea, dehydration, pregnancy, elderly or immunocompromised state, hematemesis, and inability to tolerate oral intake.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Check airway protection, mental status, vitals, orthostasis, hydration, skin perfusion, HEENT, nystagmus, papilledema, cardiac rhythm, lungs, abdomen, hernias, scars, peritoneal signs, stool/rectal when indicated, pelvic or testicular exam when appropriate, and neurologic exam. Tachycardia, orthostasis, dry mucosa, distention, high-pitched bowel sounds, papilledema, nystagmus, or focal deficits redirect the workup.

IMAGING AND ANCILLARY TESTING

Testing is targeted. Use bedside glucose, pregnancy test in women of childbearing capacity, electrolytes/renal function when volume loss is significant, urinalysis when urinary or pregnancy-related disease is possible, lipase/LFTs for pancreaticobiliary concern, VBG/ketones for DKA, drug levels when they change management, ECG/troponin for cardiac concern, and lactate or cultures when sepsis or ischemia is plausible. Every test should answer a specific red-flag branch.

Imaging follows the dangerous branch: CT head or LP for CNS concern, abdominal imaging for obstruction, perforation, ischemia, appendicitis, pancreatobiliary disease, or severe focal tenderness, pelvic ultrasound for pregnancy/adnexal disease, and CXR when pneumonia, Boerhaave syndrome, or chest pathology is in play. Rosen's algorithm is a useful safety checklist for not missing extra-GI causes.

TREATMENT

Management starts with ABCs, airway protection if mental status is poor, IV access when dehydrated or ill, crystalloid resuscitation, electrolyte replacement, treatment of the underlying diagnosis, and antiemetic selection based on likely mechanism and adverse-effect profile. Mild cases may tolerate oral rehydration after antiemetic therapy; severe dehydration, AKI, electrolyte derangement, or ongoing losses require IV management.

Disposition is part of treatment: admit or observe patients with severe dehydration, AKI, significant electrolyte derangement, persistent inability to tolerate oral intake, GI bleeding, obstruction, peritonitis, concerning neurologic/cardiac/obstetric findings, or unreliable follow-up.

ONDANSETRON

Ondansetron is a common first-line serotonin antagonist for undifferentiated nausea/vomiting. It is usually well tolerated, but dose and context matter: screen for congenital long QT, interacting QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradyarrhythmia, and significant cardiac disease. QT risk rises when dehydration and electrolyte loss are untreated.

GASTROPARESIS

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction. Diabetes is classic, but causes also include idiopathic disease, post-surgical states, viral illness, reflux/nonulcer dyspepsia, connective tissue or neurologic disease, pregnancy, and medication effects, especially opioids and anticholinergic agents. Do not label a first severe episode as gastroparesis until obstruction and metabolic emergencies are considered.

DIAGNOSIS

Symptoms include early satiety, bloating, postprandial nausea, vomiting, reflux, and abdominal pain; severe chronic disease causes weight loss, electrolyte abnormalities, and nutritional deficiencies. ED evaluation focuses on hydration, electrolytes, glucose/ketones, pregnancy, medication triggers, and imaging if obstruction or another acute abdominal process is possible.

TREATMENT

Treat with fluids, electrolyte correction, antiemetics, and prokinetic therapy such as metoclopramide when appropriate. Avoid opioids when possible because they worsen motility. Discharge only after improvement and oral tolerance or a reliable plan; persistent dehydration, AKI, electrolyte derangement, or diagnostic uncertainty needs observation or admission.

CYCLIC VOMITING SYNDROME

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Cyclic vomiting syndrome produces recurrent stereotyped episodes separated by baseline health. It overlaps with migraine biology, autonomic symptoms, and functional gut-brain disorders. Chronic cannabis exposure can produce cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome, which often resembles CVS and may be associated with hot bathing behavior.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen Ch.25 expands Tintinalli Ch.72 by separating critical, emergent, and nonemergent causes, adding CHS/CVS criteria, sequelae, and a management algorithm; Tintinalli keeps the ED spine concise with gastroparesis, cyclic vomiting, and antiemetic selection.

DIAGNOSIS

Diagnosis requires recognizing the recurrent pattern while excluding dangerous acute causes during the ED visit. Ask about prior identical episodes, triggers, migraine history, cannabis use, hot showers, symptom-free intervals, dehydration, abdominal pain, pregnancy, drug ingestion, and prior workups. Known CVS or CHS does not protect the patient from a new emergency.

TREATMENT

ED treatment is supportive: IV fluids, electrolyte replacement, antiemetics, analgesia when appropriate, benzodiazepines in selected refractory cases, and trigger counseling. CHS treatment requires cannabis cessation counseling; recurrent severe disease needs outpatient follow-up for prevention strategy.
